name: Wendy Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, 27, and I manage the marketing content team at the head office of a big washing machine and fridge maker. There are five of us: two writers, two designers and me. I share a flat with my friend Ines, who's a physiotherapist, and I'm single, which is fine, I'm mostly at work anyway. My savings got wiped out when I moved flats in the summer, so I'm starting from almost zero again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days I'm planning campaigns, reviewing what the team writes, and arguing with the product people about what we're allowed to say. A fridge is a fridge, so the job is making the energy rating sound exciting. I use AI every day, for first drafts, product descriptions in six languages and turning long reports into short posts. I love the creative bit and I'm honestly a bit addicted to new tools. What wears me out is the sign-off chain, eleven people approving one social media post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I was a bit over-excited, fair enough. I'd post something like this: Turns out AI is a very good intern, not a new boss. At work I'd keep saying it's still worth using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved and a bit bored. My team would still be needed, and my job would be the same, which is safe but a bit stuck. The real problem would still be money: I'm on the low end of the pay band and starting again from nothing after the move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools for drafts and translations, and push to get the sign-off chain shorter. I'd set up a standing order of a hundred a month into savings. And I'd look at a small freelance gig writing product copy for local businesses, maybe one evening a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, a bit itchy about everything else. I'd want more money, not less change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the AI actually save you each week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The six-language product pages used to take the agency two weeks and a lot of money. Now we do a first pass in an afternoon and get a native speaker to check it. That saving is probably why my team still exists, ironically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you find the freelance work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines's clinic needs a website refresh, so that's one. There's a bike shop and a bakery on our street with terrible websites. Fifty here and there would add up.

say: AI turns out to be **a very good intern**, not a new boss.
think: My job is **safe but stuck**, which is a bit boring.
**Money** is the real problem after the flat move wiped out savings.
do: Keep using AI for **drafts and translations**, and shorten sign-offs.
Set up a **hundred a month** standing order into savings.
Take **freelance copy** work one evening a week.
feel: **Calm about the job**, itchy about money and wanting more.
S0.quote: Turns out AI is a very good intern, not a new boss.
fieldNote: She is **comfortable with AI** and already sees it shaping her team.
Her worry is **money**, not the job, after a costly move.
She's quick to find **side income** from local businesses.

steps.text: Keep producing translated product pages with AI drafts
Set up a hundred a month standing order into savings
Redo the website copy for Ines's clinic and the bike shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say marketing is changing and that's fine, we adapt. At work I'd pitch running a smaller team that does far more. Online I'd post about how I use the tools, because that's how you get noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, writing is the first thing on that card, and that's my team. I could probably do the work of all five of us with the tools by myself, and the company would see that too. Then the question is whether they need me or just a cheaper junior with good prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who runs AI content for the whole company, not just my team. I'd try to move one writer into customer research, actually visiting homes to see how people use the machines, because that's not something AI does from a desk. And I'd quietly update my CV and look at roles in the city, even though it's ninety minutes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and worried at the same time. I love the tools, and I'd hate to be replaced by someone who loves them more and costs less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren, our older writer, who's brilliant at headlines and refuses to touch AI. Darren would be gone first, and I'd hate it. I'd try to get Darren into customer research, because he's great with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move to the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to that, yes. I have no kids and no mortgage, it's the easiest time in my life to move. The problem is a deposit, which I don't have.

say: Marketing is changing, and that's fine; **we adapt**.
I'd post about how I **use the tools** to get noticed.
think: **Writing** is first on the card, and that's my team.
The company might want a **cheaper junior** with good prompts, not me.
do: Become the company-wide lead for **AI content**.
Move a writer into **customer research** visiting homes.
Update my CV and look at **city jobs**, ninety minutes away.
feel: **Excited and worried** about being replaced by someone cheaper.
S1.quote: I could probably do the work of all five of us with the tools by myself, and the company would see that too.
fieldNote: She is unusually **honest** that the tools make her own team unnecessary.
Her answer is to **grow her remit** before someone cheaper takes it.
She sees **home visits** as work AI can't do from a desk.

steps.text: Pitch to lead AI content for the whole company
Apply for marketing jobs in the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be honest that office jobs are going first, not factory jobs. At work I'd tell the team straight. Online I'd share what I was doing so other people could use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, marketing content is one of the easiest things for AGI to do, and the factory floor would outlast me, which is a strange thing to be jealous of. My job would be gone within the first year, and the team before that. The factory floor making the washing machines would last until the robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next two years I'd build up freelance work, so I have clients who know me and not just a company. I'd look at moving into something hands-on but creative, like a photography or video business, because people still want someone holding the camera for a while. And I'd cut my spending and maybe move back to my mum's to save rent for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but buzzing a bit too. Two years is terrifying, but I'd rather jump than be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said photography. Do you have any experience?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, I shoot most of our product photos when the agency budget runs out. A decent camera is about eight hundred, which I don't have. I'd probably buy it second-hand and pay it off over a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could you go without pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two weeks, honestly. That's why moving back to my mum's matters. Rent-free for a year would mean I could save most of my last salary.

say: We need to admit **office jobs** go first, not factory jobs.
I'd **share my plan** online so others could use it.
think: **Marketing content** is easy for AGI; my job goes within a year.
Factory workers last until robots, **a strange thing** to envy.
do: Build **freelance clients** in the two years before.
Start a **photography or video** side business with a second-hand camera.
Move back to **my mum's** for a year to save rent.
feel: **Alarmed** but buzzing, preferring to jump rather than be pushed.
S2.quote: Marketing content is one of the easiest things for AGI to do, and the factory floor would outlast me, which is a strange thing to be jealous of.
fieldNote: She notices the **reversal**: factory work outlasts her desk.
She'd jump to **hands-on creative** work like photography.
Her **two weeks** of savings makes moving home essential.

steps.text: Build a list of freelance copywriting clients over two years
Buy a second-hand camera and start product photography
Move back to her mum's for a year to save rent
Cut spending to essentials until the move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead if you start now. I'd post a lot about how to use these tools, maybe even start a small newsletter. At work I'd tell the team, learn this now or regret it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd assume my role is gone by 2031. But five years is enough time to build something of my own. I'd be 32, single or not, and I'd want a business that doesn't depend on one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small content and photography business on the side, aiming to cover my rent from it by 2029. I'd move to the city once I had savings, because there are more clients there. And I'd keep using every new tool at work, so I learn on the company's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but energised. It's a race, and I'm not bad at races.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the side business doesn't take off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost a few hundred and some weekends. I'd still have learned a lot. I'd rather try and fail at 29 than wait and be stuck at 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, a bit, and Ines, who'd probably let me be late on rent once. I'd not want any help from the government, not because I'm against it, but because it'd mean things went really wrong.

say: Five years is **enough to get ahead** if you start now.
I'd tell the team: **learn this now** or regret it.
think: I want a **business of my own**, not one employer.
At 32, I'd want income that **doesn't depend** on one company.
do: Build a **content and photography** business covering rent by 2029.
Move to **the city** once there are savings.
Use every new tool at work to **learn on company time**.
feel: **Worried but energised**, treating it like a race.
S3.quote: I'd rather try and fail at 29 than wait and be stuck at 32.
fieldNote: She frames the five years as **a race** she can win.
Her fallback people are **her mum** and her flatmate Ines.
Learning on **company time** is a shrewd money-saving move.

steps.text: Grow a content and photography business to cover rent by 2029
Move to the city once three months are saved
Try every new AI tool the company rolls out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and I'd be using all of it. I'd encourage friends to plan rather than worry. I'd probably be the annoying one with the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me feel pretty good. I'd have time to build a career in something that mixes people, cameras and real places. The end point still scares me a bit, but by then I'd have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my job for three or four years, learning all I can, and save properly. Then I'd move into video production or customer research, roles with a hands-on side that last until about 2039. Once I had six months saved, I'd put a bit into an index fund each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little uneasy. It's far enough away that I'd plan, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 40 by then. Nobody knows what the world looks like after 2039, when the robots arrive too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move or buy somewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rent in the city for a few years, then maybe buy something small. I wouldn't buy until I knew I had income that wasn't just a desk job.

say: Ten years is **generous**, and I'd use all of it.
I'd urge friends to **plan rather than worry**.
think: Ten years lets me build a career mixing **people and cameras**.
The end point still **scares** me a bit, but I'd have options.
do: Stay three or four years and **save properly**.
Move into **video production** or customer research later.
Put money into an **index fund** after six months are saved.
S4.quote: Nobody knows what the world looks like after 2039, when the robots arrive too.
fieldNote: The decade turns her fear into a **career plan**.
She'd only **invest** once a cushion exists.
Her remaining worry is **after 2039**, not the next few years.

steps.text: Save steadily while staying in marketing for three or four years
Move into a video production or customer research job
Invest a little in an index fund each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the one that worries me most. Writing is my whole job and I've got two weeks of money. What would help is a cheap way to get a business started, like small grants or loans for people retraining, and time off work to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people with no partner. When you're single, there's no second income to lean on, it's just you and your rent.

headlineQuote: When you're single, there's no second income to lean on, it's just you and your rent.
portrait: Wendy is 27 and manages a **five-person content team** at a washing machine and fridge maker.
She's single, shares a flat, and **wiped out her savings** moving this summer.
She uses AI daily and openly admits it could do **her whole team's work**.
Her plan in each AGI picture is **side income** and moving toward hands-on creative work.
She is anxious or alarmed in the fast pictures but **energised** by the challenge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because writing goes first and she has two weeks saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Small grants or loans** to start a business while retraining.
**Time off work** to learn new skills.
